Male upland bully (Gobiomorphus breviceps) attain a maximum total length of 8.2 cm [Li = 8.2 cm], a modest size typical of small benthic eleotrids inhabiting New Zealand's freshwater systems. This ultimate length is achieved following an extended period of somatic growth that proceeds slowly in the cool, stenothermal environments the species favours. Field collections from South Island streams consistently yield gravid females during the austral spring, with egg diameters of approximately 2.7 mm recorded from dissected ovaries. The wet weight at birth, derived from these ovoid eggs, is approximately 0.01 g [Wwb = approximately 0.01 g], representing the initial mass from which larvae commence their development. Newly hatched prolarvae possess a prominent yolk sac and remain endotrophic for several days before transitioning to exogenous feeding. Their small size at eclosion places them among the more diminutive freshwater teleost neonates and likely constrains early survival in habitats with abundant invertebrate predators.

Reproductive maturation in Gobiomorphus breviceps begins when individuals reach a total length of 3.2 cm [Lp = 3.2 cm], a size attained during the first year of life under typical thermal conditions. At this developmental milestone, the gonads initiate gametogenesis and individuals become morphologically distinguishable as males or females. The corresponding body mass at puberty is 0.34 g [Wwp = 0.34 g], a figure estimated from length-weight regressions applied to field-caught specimens. This relatively low mass at the onset of reproductive capability reflects a life-history strategy that favours early maturation, likely an adaptation to unpredictable stream environments where adult mortality can be high. Juveniles transitioning through this pubertal stage exhibit rapidly accelerating growth rates, diverting resources toward both somatic increase and the initial stages of gonadal development. The size advantage gained during this period is critical for securing suitable nesting territories on the stream bed.

At a stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], a temperature that approximates the annual mean in many of the species' native habitats, the maximum reproductive rate of the upland bully has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions. Females under these thermal conditions achieve a sustained annual reproductive output of approximately 400 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 400 eggs per year], corresponding to a daily rate of approximately 1.1 eggs per day sustained over several weeks of continuous spawning activity. This output is achieved through repeated ovarian cycles, with each gravid female producing clutches of approximately 200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 200 eggs per clutch] and producing approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year] of adhesive eggs deposited onto the undersides of cobbles, which are then guarded by the attending male until eclosion. The rate represents the highest sustained fecundity observed in this species and likely approaches the physiological maximum permitted by the energetic constraints of a cool-water existence. Field observations confirm that such rates are attainable only when prey availability is high.

Marked sexual dimorphism in body size is characteristic of this eleotrid, with males reaching an ultimate wet weight of 5.88 g [Wwi = 5.88 g], considerably greater than the asymptotic mass attained by females. This difference supports the species' polygynous mating system, in which larger males control superior nesting sites and receive spawning visits from multiple females. The ultimate wet weight corresponds closely to the value predicted by the length-weight relationship derived from the male asymptotic length. Among New Zealand's freshwater fish fauna, this species occupies an intermediate position in terms of maximum adult mass, being heavier than the smaller Galaxias species but substantially lighter than large anguillid eels. This body size influences metabolic rate, diet composition, and vulnerability to piscivorous birds and eels that share its stream habitat.

Longevity in the upland bully, as documented from both mark-recapture studies and captive-maintained individuals, reaches a maximum of approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years] under the thermal regime typical of its southern distribution (14 °C [T = 14 °C]). This lifespan, equivalent to about 1,642 days [am = about 1,642 days] at 14 °C, places Gobiomorphus breviceps among the shorter-lived freshwater eleotrids, contrasting with congeneric species that may persist for a decade or more in more stable lacustrine environments at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. The relatively brief lifespan is associated with high adult metabolic costs incurred during the extended breeding season and the energetic demands of nest-guarding behaviour. Senescence becomes apparent in individuals beyond three years of age, manifesting as reduced condition factor and diminished spawning success.
